messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 57

# Vignette: Emmanuel

Emmanuel is a 62-year-old married man who has spent the better part of four decades doing work that most people cannot bring themselves to imagine. As a bomb disposal technician, he has always understood that danger is simply part of the contract — something to be managed through training, discipline, and the kind of quiet courage that never announces itself. He has defused devices in the field, worked in conditions that would paralyze an ordinary person, and come home each time to his wife, Amara, and their grown children. For most of his career, he believed that his composure was something close to permanent.

That belief ended three years ago.

During a routine sweep of a suspected weapons storage facility, Emmanuel and two colleagues encountered what appeared to be a compromised canister of industrial chemical agent. Before proper containment protocols could be executed, there was a partial release. Emmanuel was closest to the source. He remembers the smell first — something sweet and wrong at the same time — and then a burning sensation across his face and throat that arrived before he had time to reach for his mask. He was evacuated, decontaminated, and hospitalized for eleven days. His colleagues were treated and discharged within a week. Emmanuel's respiratory damage was more significant, and the uncertainty about long-term effects was never fully resolved by the medical team.

He returned to modified administrative duties within three months, insisting to his supervisors and to Amara that he was fine. He was not fine.

The smell is the thing that undoes him most reliably. Cleaning products, certain perfumes, even the particular sharpness of cold morning air can send him back to that room with a speed and completeness that leaves him gripping whatever surface is nearest. During these moments, Emmanuel does not feel as though he is remembering — he feels as though he is still there, still breathing something that is trying to kill him. His heart pounds, his throat tightens, and for a few seconds that feel much longer, he is certain he is dying. He has stopped using the communal kitchen at work because a colleague's solvent-based hand cleaner triggered an episode so severe that he had to leave the building and sit in his car for forty minutes before he could drive.

At home, Amara has learned not to light scented candles. She has not said anything about this directly, and neither has he, but they both know. Emmanuel finds himself checking the windows before bed — not for intruders, but to make sure nothing is getting in. He sleeps in fragments, waking between two and four in the morning with his chest tight and his mind already running through the sequence of events at the facility, searching, as it always does, for the moment where he could have done something differently. He has not found it. He keeps looking.

He is quieter than he used to be. His eldest son mentioned it at a family dinner, framing it gently as a question about whether his father was tired, and Emmanuel changed the subject with the practiced ease of a man who has spent a lifetime managing what others see. What his son does not know is that Emmanuel had excused himself to the bathroom twenty minutes earlier because the smell of the gas stove had made his hands shake.

He still goes to work. He still reads the technical briefings, still consults on cases, still presents himself as a man with thirty-eight years of experience who knows what he is doing. And in many respects, he does. But he also knows that he has not been inside an active disposal site since the incident, and that when his supervisor recently suggested he might return to light field work, Emmanuel agreed immediately and then spent the following night awake until dawn, watching the ceiling and telling himself that he would be ready.

He is not sure he believes it.
